Improvement of stiff-person syndrome
with tiagabine
Beth B. Murinson, MD, PhD; and Marco Rizzo, MD, PhD
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS), a neurologic disorder of severe pro-
gressive stiffness and spasms of legs and spine, is frequently asso-
ciated with the production of autoimmune antibodies.
1
Immunologic therapies, including plasmapheresis and IV immu-
noglobulin, usually do not produce a permanent improvement in
symptoms and treatment frequently requires benzodiazepines.
2,3
High-dose benzodiazepine therapy is effective, but is often worri-
some, particularly in patients who do not have a positive antibody
test to support the clinical diagnosis. To date, three autoantigens
have been associated with SPS.
4 It is likely that there are patients
in whom specific antibodies are not yet identified. We present an
antibody-negative patient with clinical SPS whose symptoms im-
proved significantly in response to the anticonvulsant tiagabine,
an inhibitor of GABA catabolism.
5
Case report. A 39-year-old woman presented with an 8-year
history of progressive stiffness and spasm of lower extremities,
abdomen, and spine. Stiffness of the neck and spine first occurred
with a febrile episode; subsequently she experienced progressive
stiffness. Episodes of painful spasm occurred several times a
month. The symptoms became more disabling and 3 years before
admission she discontinued work. Diazepam was effective but re-
quired gradually increasing doses. Carbamazepine lessened her
pain but not the stiffness, baclofen was transiently effective in
reducing severe stiffness, and lorazepam and clonazepam were
less effective than diazepam. Immunomodulating therapies had
not been tried.
On initial examination the patient was awake and able to
provide a detailed history. She was lying in bed with legs in stiff
extensor posture, arms in modified flexor posture, spine hyperlor-
dotic, and muscles of the abdomen hard. The plantar response was
extensor; sensation and coordination were intact. Sudden noise
provoked spasm and increased stiffness. Administration of IV di-
azepam produced drowsiness and relief of stiffness such that the
patient attained a seated posture and propelled a wheelchair.
EMG showed involuntary continuous motor unit activity of
agonist–antagonist muscle groups consistent with SPS. The se-
rum was negative for antibodies to glutamic acid decarboxylase,
amphiphysin, and gephyrin. MRI of the brain and spinal cord

showed increased lumbar lordosis but were otherwise normal.
CSF, mammogram, and thoracic CT were unremarkable.
Daily administration of tiagabine 4 mg was introduced during
hospitalization. Initially the diazepam dose was 60 mg daily and
clonazepam was 4.5 mg daily. Seven days after initiation of tiaga-
bine, diazepam was tapered by 10 mg every 3 days to a dose of 10
mg daily. Over the subsequent 3 months tiagabine was titrated to
6 mg daily; diazepam ranged from 5 to 15 mg daily. At her first
follow-up visit the patient demonstrated markedly reduced tone
including face, arms, and legs. The patient had difficulty standing
because she was used to locking her knees to ambulate and could
not do so; strength in the lower extremities was mildly decreased.
After 2 months of rehabilitation she was able to walk with bilat-
eral cane support.
Discussion. Initially we chose a dose of tiagabine substan-
tially lower than that used to treat epilepsy because tiagabine
should be a potent potentiator of diazepam. In fact the response
was dramatic; when this patient received 6 mg of tiagabine daily,
her use of diazepam was reduced tenfold. At higher doses of tiaga-
bine, as much as 12 mg per day, the patient experienced somno-
lence, lightheadedness, and subjectively slowed cognition. Side
effects were less pronounced with a twice-daily dosing regimen.
It has been hypothesized that a decrease in synaptic GABA in
the spinal cord can result in symptoms of SPS, thereby explaining
prior success in treatment with benzodiazepines, baclofen, and
vigabatrin. Because an increase in synaptic GABA is expected to
complement a noncompetitive GABA agonist, such as diazepam, it
has been suggested that tiagabine may be effective in SPS.
6 By
treating our patient with tiagabine, we reduced the dosage and
toxicity of diazepam while markedly improving mobility and func-
tion. Tiagabine added at low doses may be effective in reducing a
diazepam requirement severalfold.

The cystatin C polymorphism is not associated
with early onset Alzheimer’s disease

G. Roks, MD; M. Cruts, PhD; A.J.C. Slooter, PhD;
B. Dermaut, MD; A. Hofman, MD, PhD;
C. Van Broeckhoven, PhD; and C.M. Van Duijn, PhD
There is growing evidence that vascular factors are involved in
AD.
1 In light of these findings, a polymorphism in the cystatin C
gene (CST3) that was recently found to be associated with late
onset AD is a promising candidate gene.
2 Cystatin C is an amyloi-
dogenic protein found together with b-amyloid in the arteriolar
walls of patients with AD and patients with congophilic amyloid
angiopathy (CAA).
3 As CAA is also a prominent feature in early
onset AD and Down syndrome4 and a mutation in cystatin C leads
to CAA at very early age 5 we investigated the role of the CST3
polymorphism in early onset AD.
Methods. Patients were derived from a population-based study
of early onset AD in the Netherlands, as described in detail be-
fore.
6 AD was diagnosed using a protocol in accordance with the
National Institute of Neurological and Communicative Disorders
and Stroke–Alzheimer’s Disease and Related Disorders Associa-
tion criteria.
7 Of the 198 patients ascertained, 101 were available
for DNA analysis. From these 101 patients, 56 had a positive
family history, 11 had a family history compatible with an autoso-
mal dominant inheritance pattern, and 34 were sporadic patients.
Controls were derived from the Rotterdam Study.
1 They were
randomly drawn from subjects in the age category of 55 to 65
years. All controls were screened on cognitive function and sub-
jects who were suspected of having dementia were excluded,
1 re-
sulting in a control group of 117 individuals.
The CST3 and APOE polymorphisms were determined as de-
scribed previously. 2,6 Genotype and allele frequencies were com-

pared between cases and controls with the chi-square statistic.
The odds ratio for AD associated with the CST3 GG genotype was
computed using an age, gender, and education level adjusted lo-
gistic regression model, using the GA and AA groups as a refer-
ence category. Possible interaction with age or APOE were
explored by stratification (median age of 58 used as cut-off) and by
testing for multiplicative interaction, using a product term in the
logistic regression model.
Results. The mean age at AD onset was 57 years (SD 5 5.0),
which was lower than the age in the controls (mean 61 years, SD
5 3.3, t-test p , 0.01). The patient group included a larger propor-
tion of women compared to controls (77% versus 55%, x

p , 0.01). The CST3 genotype frequencies were, in both cases and
controls, in Hardy Weinberg equilibrium (controls p 5 0.80; cases
p 5 0.30). The table shows the genotype and allele frequencies of
the CST3 polymorphism. We found no association between the
CST3 genotype and early onset AD overall. The age, gender, and
education adjusted odds ratio for early onset AD associated with
the GG genotype was 1.1 (95% confidence interval 0.5, 2.4). There
was no evidence for a statistical interaction between the CST3
polymorphism and age (p 5 0.82). After stratification according to
age, the GG frequency was slightly higher in older cases (table),
but far from statistically significant. There was also no evidence
for a statistical interaction between the CST3 and APOE polymor-
phisms (p 5 0.69).
Discussion. In this population-based study of early onset AD,
we did not find an association with the CST3 GG genotype. In a
previous study, the CST3 GG genotype was found to be associated
with very late onset AD.
2 AD aggregates strongly in families even
at very old ages. This is only partly explained by APOE*4, sug-
gesting that there are unknown late onset AD genes. However, it
is doubtful whether CST3 is a gene related to the risk of AD. In
the study of Crawford et al. there was only a borderline significant
effect in the oldest age group.
2 Because cystatin C is a protein
involved in CAA, which is also present in early onset AD, there is
no a priori hypothesis that the cystatin C gene is more important
in late onset AD. The absence of an association to early forms of
AD in the study of Crawford et al.
2 and the current study argues
against a causal relationship. Another problem in the interpreta-
tion of the study of Crawford et al.
2 is that the association between
the CST3 gene and AD resulted mainly from a decrease in GG
frequency in the controls. This finding suggests a role of the CST3
gene in another competing disorder rather than in AD.
